corpus_definition: To start to rot or become bad to eat.
particle_note: Not separable and has no object: 'The milk has gone off.' Mainly British English; American English usually says 'go bad'.

relations.note: Same meaning; more common in American English.
A little more formal: 'The fish will spoil in the heat.'
Stronger: food that rots is completely bad and often smells.
Used mainly for milk that starts to taste bad.

context.text: It was very hot in Tashkent, and the milk went off in one day. Put the meat in the fridge, or it will go off too.

reviewer_note: Only the food sense; other senses of go off (an alarm rings, a bomb explodes, someone leaves) are not included.

corpus_definition: To talk about other people's private lives.

forms.definition: talk or stories about other people's private lives
forms.example: I never listen to office gossip about my colleagues.
forms.note: Also used for a person who likes to talk about others: 'She is a terrible gossip.'

syn.note: A story that may not be true and spreads from person to person. American spelling: rumor.
Friendly, informal talk; not always about other people.

forms.definition: to talk about other people's private lives, often unkindly
forms.example: People love to gossip at the office party.

syn.note: Easy word: to talk in a friendly way, not always about other people.
To talk quickly and a lot about unimportant things.
British and informal: to talk for a long time about small things.

forms.definition: liking to talk about other people's private lives
forms.example: Our gossipy neighbour knows everything about everyone on the street.

syn.note: Likes to talk a lot, but not always about other people.
Talks a lot; a neutral word.

ant.note: Careful not to tell other people's secrets.

forms.note: No common adverb in learner dictionaries.

context.text: My aunts love to gossip over tea. They share all the gossip from the mahalla, but my grandmother says it is not kind to be so gossipy.

reviewer_note: The person sense of gossip (same spelling) is only in the noun note, not repeated in People & things.

corpus_definition: A large round yellow citrus fruit with a tart pink or red center.

forms.definition: a large round yellow citrus fruit with a sour, slightly bitter taste
forms.example: I drink fresh grapefruit juice every morning for breakfast.
forms.note: The plural is grapefruit or grapefruits.

syn.note: The group of fruits that grapefruit belongs to, with oranges and lemons.
A similar fruit, but bigger and sweeter.

context.text: I eat half a grapefruit for breakfast. It is a bit sour, so my little brother always adds some honey to his grapefruit.

reviewer_note: Single-word food noun; no family forms exist. Not linked to grape.

corpus_definition: To understand something that is hard to learn.

forms.definition: how well you understand a subject or situation
forms.example: She has a very good grasp of English grammar.

syn.note: Easy, general word with almost the same meaning.
What you know; grasp is about how well you understand it.
Used for languages and skills: 'a good command of English'.

forms.definition: to understand something, especially something difficult
forms.example: He could not grasp the main idea of the lesson.

syn.note: Easy, everyday word with the same meaning.
Formal, often in writing.
Informal: 'I don't get it.'
To understand an explanation while you listen to it.

ant.note: To understand something in the wrong way.

forms.definition: always trying to get more money or things
forms.example: The grasping landlord raised the rent again.
forms.note: Belongs to grasp = try to take and hold things, here money; it means greedy, not understanding.

context.text: At first, Dilnoza could not grasp the new maths topic. After a week of practice, she has a much better grasp of it.

reviewer_note: Map keeps the 'understand' sense only; the physical 'hold tightly' sense of grasp is left out. grasping (greedy) is other_meaning.

corpus_definition: A strong wish to have more food, money, or things than needed.

forms.definition: a strong wish to have more money, food or things than you need
forms.example: His greed for gold led to his ruin.

syn.note: Formal word, used for money and riches.
Thinking only about yourself, not only about having more.

ant.note: Being happy to give money, time or things to others.

forms.definition: the quality of always wanting more than you need
forms.example: Everyone in the village talked about the merchant's greediness.

forms.definition: wanting more money, food or things than you need
forms.example: The greedy boy ate all the sweets and gave none to his sister.

syn.note: Easy word: thinking only about yourself.
Caring too much about money and things you can buy.
Always trying to get more money; a stronger, more negative word.

ant.note: Happy to give money, food or time to others.

forms.definition: in a way that shows you want more than you need
forms.example: The children ate the cake greedily.

syn.note: Used mainly about eating fast because you are very hungry.
In a way that thinks only about yourself.

ant.note: In a way that gives a lot to others.

context.text: My little brother ate all the plov greedily. Mum told him that greed is a bad habit and that greedy children do not get dessert.

reviewer_note: greed is the base and greedy is made from it with -y; greediness kept as a less common extra noun.

corpus_definition: Extreme sadness, especially when someone you love dies.

forms.definition: very great sadness, especially when someone you love dies
forms.example: He felt great grief after his mother died.

syn.note: A little formal; deep sadness for any reason.
Easy, general word; grief is much stronger.
The time and customs of showing sadness after a death.
Strong sadness, often about love.

forms.definition: a complaint about something that you think is unfair
forms.example: The workers met the manager to discuss their grievances.
forms.note: Belongs to grief = feeling unfairly treated, not sadness after a death.

forms.definition: to feel very sad because someone you love has died
forms.example: The whole village grieved for the old teacher.

syn.note: Same meaning; often also means showing your sadness in public.
Formal or literary: to show sadness, often with words.

ant.note: To feel or show great happiness; a little formal.

forms.definition: feeling very sad because someone has died
forms.example: The grieving family thanked everyone who came to the funeral.

syn.note: Extremely sad; also used about love.
Very sad; a literary word.

forms.definition: very serious and causing great harm or pain
forms.example: The driver made a grievous mistake.
forms.note: Belongs to grief = serious harm, not sadness after a death. Formal; often in law: grievous bodily harm.

forms.definition: very seriously or badly
forms.example: He was grievously injured in the accident.
forms.note: Goes with grievous (serious harm), not sadness. Formal.

context.text: After her grandfather died, Madina was full of grief. The whole family grieved together, and the neighbours brought food to the grieving family.

reviewer_note: grievance, grievous, grievously share the root but belong to the 'harm / unfair' meaning, so they are other_meaning.

corpus_definition: To crush something into small pieces or powder.

forms.definition: hard, boring work that goes on for a long time
forms.example: After the holiday, it was back to the daily grind.
forms.note: Belongs to grind = tiring, boring work, not crushing food. Informal; usually 'the daily grind'.

forms.definition: to crush something into very small pieces or powder
forms.example: They grind coffee beans to make fresh drinks.

syn.note: Press hard to break into pieces; the pieces may be bigger.
Grind grain or coffee, often with a machine.
Hit many times to break something, for example in a bowl.
Break something soft, like bread, into small pieces with your fingers.

forms.definition: crushed into very small pieces or powder
forms.example: Add a spoon of ground black pepper to the soup.
forms.note: Don't confuse with the noun ground (the earth under your feet).

syn.note: Made into powder: powdered milk, powdered sugar.
Broken by pressing; pieces can be bigger.

ant.note: Whole spices or beans are not crushed.

forms.definition: very hard and tiring, and seeming to never end
forms.example: Many families lived in grinding poverty.
forms.note: Belongs to grind = hard, tiring work, not crushing food. Often in 'grinding poverty'.

people.definition: a machine or tool that crushes coffee, pepper or meat
people.example: We bought an electric grinder for our coffee beans.

context.text: My father grinds coffee beans every morning with a small grinder. He says freshly ground coffee tastes much better.

reviewer_note: Trap: participle 'ground' is spelled like the noun ground (earth); noted. Noun grind (daily grind) is other_meaning.

corpus_definition: To hold something very tightly with your hand.

forms.definition: a tight hold on something with your hand
forms.example: She kept a firm grip on the rope.

syn.note: Easy, general word; a hold can be gentle.
A firm hold; also used for understanding.
A tight hold, often of someone's hand.

forms.definition: to hold something very tightly with your hand
forms.example: Grip the handle tightly when the bus starts moving.

syn.note: Easy, general word; you can hold something gently.
Take and hold firmly.
Hold tightly, often because you are afraid.
Hold tightly, often hands or someone in your arms.

ant.note: Easy phrase: to stop holding something.

forms.definition: so exciting that it holds your attention completely
forms.example: It was a gripping film, and nobody left early.
forms.note: Belongs to grip = hold your attention, not holding with your hand.

context.text: Grandpa Bobur still has a strong grip. He can grip a heavy bag of potatoes and carry it all the way home from the bazaar.

reviewer_note: gripping (exciting) is other_meaning; noun grip is a same-spelling conversion.

corpus_definition: A person who sells food and small household items in a shop.

forms.definition: a person who owns or works in a shop that sells food
forms.example: I bought fresh fruit from the local grocer today.
forms.note: The grocer's = the grocer's shop (British English).

syn.note: Any person who owns a small shop, not only a food shop. American English: storekeeper.

people.definition: a shop that sells food and things for the house
people.example: There is a small grocery at the end of our street.
people.note: The plural groceries means the food and things you buy there: 'I carried the groceries home.'

context.text: Our local grocer opens at seven every morning. My mother buys all her groceries there because the prices are fair.

reviewer_note: Headword is a person noun, so it stays the main noun entry; grocery (shop) and groceries (food) go in People & things. greengrocer is a compound, left out.

corpus_definition: To make a low, rough sound in the throat.

forms.definition: a low, rough sound from the throat, often of an angry animal
forms.example: We heard a growl from behind the gate.

syn.note: An angry sound, usually with the teeth showing.
A long, low sound, like thunder or a hungry stomach.

forms.definition: to make a low, rough sound in the throat, often angrily
forms.example: The hungry dog began to growl softly.
forms.note: People can growl too: to say something in a low, angry voice.

syn.note: Make an angry sound while showing the teeth.
Make a long, low sound: 'My stomach is rumbling.'
A much louder sound, like a lion.

forms.definition: making a low, rough sound in the throat
forms.example: The growling dog would not let us into the yard.

syn.note: Angry and showing its teeth.

context.text: Our neighbour's dog growls at everyone who walks past. Last night I heard a loud growl and saw the growling dog near our gate.

reviewer_note: Not related to grow; growl is its own word.
